overview: The CC Community Development Board is responsible for site plan reviews, granting special permits, and recommending zoning amendments to the City Council to align Medford’s development with its 2023 Comprehensive Plan. Meeting regularly since late 2022, the board oversees large-scale commercial developments, public housing modernizations, and institutional expansions for Tufts University. Its work involves balancing neighborhood character and infrastructure capacity with state-mandated housing unit requirements and transit-oriented development goals. Most recently, the board has been finalizing citywide zoning 'cleanup' amendments and procurement for long-term planning consultants.

threads.name: Comprehensive Zoning Recodification
threads.summary: Following the adoption of the city's Comprehensive Plan in early 2023, the board embarked on a multi-year effort to modernize archaic zoning definitions and use tables. This process included hiring consultants to lead a 18-month citywide overhaul and implementing a multiplier-based 'Green Score' system to improve ecological standards for private development. The board has held dozens of workshops to align local ordinances with the city's long-term vision for housing density and climate resiliency. By late 2026, the work shifted toward a 'cleanup' phase to standardize height definitions and formatting across the newly adopted districts.

threads.name: Tufts University Institutional Development
threads.summary: The board frequently reviews institutional projects under the Dover Amendment, which limits municipal authority over educational uses while allowing for reasonable dimensional standards. Significant projects included an 8-court tennis facility, the modernization of various academic halls, and a highly debated 10-story, 677-bed dormitory at 401 Boston Avenue. The board eventually approved the 401 Boston Avenue site plan with conditions for annual reporting on shuttle usage and community fund transparency. Recent efforts have focused on creating a dedicated 'Institutional Zoning District' for the Tufts campus to establish clearer boundaries and height transitions near residential areas.

threads.name: Medford Housing Authority Modernization
threads.summary: The board has overseen the comprehensive modernization of major public housing facilities, beginning with a 222-unit overhaul of the Saltonstall building at 121 Riverside Avenue. A major effort involved the redevelopment of Walkling Court into 238 deeply affordable units, which required the recommendation of a new Planned Development District (PDD-3). The board approved modified site plans for these projects as financing and land acquisitions from state agencies necessitated changes to parking and circulation layouts. These approvals were often conditioned on contributions to city funds or improvements to adjacent greenway paths.

threads.name: Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs)
threads.summary: The board initially managed the city's first ADU permits through individual special permit applications for detached garage conversions and legalizing existing units. Following changes to Massachusetts state law, the board transitioned to developing a comprehensive local regulatory framework for 'protected' ADUs. These new regulations addressed size caps, physical typologies, and the elimination of owner-occupancy or transit-adjacent parking requirements. Public sessions focused on helping residents understand if small lots could physically accommodate such units under the new density standards.

threads.name: MBTA Communities & Wellington Transit Overlay
threads.summary: To comply with state mandates for multi-family housing near transit, the board developed the Wellington Station Multifamily Overlay District. Deliberations focused on modeling unit capacity and balancing transit goals with local car dependency through reduced parking minimums and maximums. The final recommendation to the City Council included a parking minimum of 0.5 spaces per unit to achieve a theoretical capacity of over 6,000 units. Subsequent amendments were recommended to refine setbacks, green standards, and definitions for building coverage within the overlay.

threads.name: Commercial Transit Corridor Zoning
threads.summary: The board has systematically reviewed and recommended new zoning districts for major city corridors, including Mystic Avenue, Salem Street, and Boston Avenue. These amendments aim to transform industrial or commercial corridors into walkable, mixed-use districts with simplified dimensional standards and incentive-based building heights. The process for the Boston Avenue corridor involved extensive joint sessions with the City Council to establish standards for 'purpose-built student housing' and shadow protections for neighboring homes. While some corridor plans were tabled by the City Council, the board continues to refine mapping and height scenarios based on public feedback.

threads.name: Medford and West Medford Square Rezoning
threads.summary: Zoning updates for the city's squares focused on encouraging commercial density while protecting historic assets and sun access for neighbors. The board evaluated framework proposals for building heights ranging up to 12 stories near major highways, balanced by 45-degree height transitions at residential edges. A significant 'Transom' project overlay was recommended for the City Hall parking lot to facilitate 300 residential units and an urban grocery store. The board ultimately recommended that the City Council adopt the revised Medford Square District Zoning Amendment in April 2026.

threads.name: Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Oversight
threads.summary: The board holds annual public hearings to manage the CDBG program, covering funding priorities for infrastructure, housing rehabilitation, and public services. Accomplishments reported over several fiscal years include sidewalk installations on Arlington Street, housing rehab loans, and support for food security and senior transportation. The board also coordinates CDBG allocations with supplemental ARPA grant opportunities and reviews the Consolidated Annual Performance Evaluation Report (CAPER). Recent initiatives included establishing a Neighborhood Revitalization Strategy Area to better target resources for low-to-moderate-income communities.
